  We estimate the geothermal gradient and surface temperature from four

  that the inversion is dimensionally consistent before anything is run.

# Introduction

Inverse problems are a rich source of unit errors: the normal equations of
a least-squares fit mix entries with *different* units, and it is easy to
lose track of which is which. In this note we work through a small
inversion in fortl, where each quantity is typed with its unit of measure.

The code cells below run as the article is rendered, like a notebook: each
cell sees the definitions made in earlier cells, and under each cell we show
the type that fortl infers and the value it computes.

# Data

A borehole has thermistors at four depths:

```{.fortl}
z1 : Float[Unit[m]] = 100.0
z2 : Float[Unit[m]] = 200.0
z3 : Float[Unit[m]] = 300.0
z4 : Float[Unit[m]] = 400.0
```

and records the following (noisy) temperatures:

```{.fortl}
t1 : Float[Unit[K]] = 285.7
t2 : Float[Unit[K]] = 288.1
t3 : Float[Unit[K]] = 290.6
t4 : Float[Unit[K]] = 293.2
```

The data are plotted in @fig-fit, together with the fitted model derived
below.

![Borehole temperature measurements (points) and the least-squares fit
$T(z) = T_0 + G z$ (line).](figures/borehole-fit.svg){#fig-fit width=70%}

# Forward model and normal equations

We model temperature as linear in depth,
$$
T(z) = T_0 + G\,z,
$$
with unknown surface temperature $T_0$ and geothermal gradient $G$.
Minimising the squared misfit gives the normal equations
$$
\begin{pmatrix} n & \Sigma z \\ \Sigma z & \Sigma z^2 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} T_0 \\ G \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} \Sigma T \\ \Sigma zT \end{pmatrix}.
$$
The matrix entries have units $1$, $\mathrm{m}$ and $\mathrm{m}^2$, and the
right-hand side has units $\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{m\,K}$. In fortl, each
of these sums gets its own type:

```{.fortl}
n : Float[Unit[1]] = 4.0

sum_z   : Float[Unit[m]]     = z1 + z2 + z3 + z4
sum_zz  : Float[Unit[m^2]]   = z1*z1 + z2*z2 + z3*z3 + z4*z4
sum_t   : Float[Unit[K]]     = t1 + t2 + t3 + t4
sum_zt  : Float[Unit[m * K]] = z1*t1 + z2*t2 + z3*t3 + z4*t4
```

# Solving by Cramer's rule

The determinant has units $\mathrm{m}^2$:

```{.fortl}
det : Float[Unit[m^2]] = n * sum_zz - sum_z * sum_z
```

and Cramer's rule then gives the gradient and the surface temperature.
The type checker confirms that they come out in $\mathrm{K/m}$ and
$\mathrm{K}$ respectively:

```{.fortl}
grad : Float[Unit[K / m]] = (n * sum_zt - sum_z * sum_t) / det
```

```{.fortl}
t0 : Float[Unit[K]] = (sum_zz * sum_t - sum_z * sum_zt) / det
```

## What a unit error looks like

Suppose we mix up the terms in the numerator for the gradient. Fortl
rejects the definition before running anything. (This cell is marked
`error=true`, so the failure is expected and shown in amber.)

```{.fortl error=true}
bad_grad : Float[Unit[K / m]] = (n * sum_zz - sum_z * sum_t) / det
```

# Heat flow

Fourier's law gives the surface heat flow $q = k\,G$ in terms of the
thermal conductivity $k$ of the host rock:

```{.fortl}
conductivity : Float[Unit[J / (s * m * K)]] = 3.0
heat_flow : Float[Unit[J / (s * m^2)]] = conductivity * grad
```

that is, about $75\ \mathrm{mW\,m^{-2}}$, a typical continental value.
